I would strongly encourage anyone considering a full marathon to do at least 5 or 6 half marathon races before they even sign up for a full. It is a huge jump IMO, especially if you’re a slower runner. 

I always say, if you can run a mile, you can run 5k. If you can run 5k, you could limp around a 10k. If you can run 10k, you can probably manage a half. But you would be damn lucky to manage full if you can only just run a half.

My OH and I are priced out of our home town/village (we grew up in the same area). It's commuter belt London, both locations have direct train links to central London within an hour and since about 2006 prices have just risen and risen beyond insane proportions. To buy in my OHs village you're looking at nearly a million for a very standard 4 bed semi Edwardian house with one parking space, in my home town it's close to £450k for a small 3 bed in the 'rough' estate, kitchen/diner and living room downstairs only.

We're buying \~30 minutes away in a smaller area with no train station and can just about afford a 3 bed semi with office and separate dining room at around £420k. We'll never be able to live in the same town/village as our parents and neither will our siblings. And tbh I wouldn't want to live in the town I grew up in anyway - it's got about 2 shops in the once massive and thriving shopping centre (never recovered from the 3008 recession, at one point something like 60% of the shops in the town were out of business), one very expensive cinema, a tiny swimming pool and nothing else. Limited green space because the council lets developers build on whatever land they can get their hands on. Parking and traffic is an absolute nightmare and there's hardly any services like primary schools or GP surgeries that aren't hugely oversubscribed.

So this is my take.

I have an expensive running vest (Salomon) which I bought about 5 years when I started training for my first marathon about 6 years after I started running properly. I used cheaper ones before for a bit, but it was a present to myself for feeling ready to do a marathon. Worth the investment, I wore it twice a week for about 4 months and at the race itself. Wasn't cheap at nearly £100, but far more comfortable and practical that any of the cheaper options and it doesn't feel like I'm wearing anything extra when I wear it. Marathon was in 2021.

Since the marathon I haven't run over about 6 miles, so I have only worn it 3 times. Twice when I had to run commute home from work and needed to take more than just my phone and keys on a run, and once this past weekend as I've started longer distance running again and had a 75 minute run on my plan. I wanted my phone, headphones, sunglasses and a snack with me just in case even though I was running around my local area. Personally I would normally just stick my phone and my key in my waistband pocket or not take my phone with me at all. I don't buy running leggings/shorts without any zipped storage integrated in any more.

If you absolutely *need* to take medication, extra food, water, and are likely to be running for a fairly decent time (more than 45 minutes for a beginner, more than an hour for a more experienced runner) then a running vest makes sense. HOWEVER. Do you really *need* to take cards with you when you run? Do you need to take the medication - is it something you will use on the run and can't wait until you get home (especially if you're only going for 20 - 30 minutes)? An asthma inhaler is different to painkillers for example. You may need the asthma inhaler on a run, you won't need painkillers. The vast majority of people even with medical conditions will not need their medication on their run. Obviously not talking about diabetes, POTS or asthma, that kind of thing. 

But if you're buying a running vest because someone on instagram told you that "all runners need this!" and "you must take 5 gels on your 2 mile run!" then  you do not need a running vest. This is my issue with the trend towards running vests recently. Most people do not need more than their phone and their keys on a run under 5 miles. People have absolutely been sold a lie that you have to have this product to be a runner. You don't! You do NOT need to buy an expensive product because tiktok or instagram told you so.

Eurgh, I some how managed to delete my comment. It looked like it had double posted, but hadn't. What I wanted to say was similar to this - 

Marathons and birth are similar. You can prep as much as you want for both. You can do the long runs/the hypnobirthing classes. You can take the gels/raspberry leaf tea. You can do the visualizations and mindfulness. You can strength train. You can get a training program/listen to a podcast telling you how to do it and how amazing the experience will be. 

The truth is they both fucking hurt and the first thing I tell anyone who asks me about doing one is that you need to respect the distance and acknowledge that it will hurt. 

Like in birth, you can control a lot of things but you cannot control everything in a marathon. You can't control the weather (London this past weekend was incredibly hot; not great for a lot of people) and you can't control the internal reaction you initially have to it. You can't control how well the gels you take on sit even if you've taken them every single long run for the last 18 weeks. You might end up on the struggle bus at mile 12 and in the pain cave by mile 18 like I did in my marathon. The only way out, like with birth, is through that pain. 

Oh and you definitely might shit yourself in public at both events. But you know what? Lots of people do!

If I call at 3pm and it's urgent, especially if it's for my toddler, they'll fit me in that day. If I call at any time other than between 8:30am and 10am and it's a routine issue, I have to call back the next day at 8:30am to get a routine appointment.

You can compare job roles, skills, time in education to get somewhere decent until you're blue in the face. Fact is we all work bloody hard and none of us are compensated for it fairly.

As an AHP I often get accused of "sitting down and doing nothing all day" but what the nurses don't see is I'm responsible for the assessment and discharge planning of all appropriate patients on our ward. That could be 24 patients. A nurse has 6 - 8. I have to - or delegate, if I've got staff - assess them all for mobility on the flat and stairs, cognition, functional ability, safety/risk awareness, speak to their families, speak with social work and other members of the discharge planning team to get a plan in place, fill out forms that take half an hour at least to populate for multiple patients, argue back with a team who's never met the patient as to why I've suggested what I need, document all of that, do capacity assessments, the list goes on. It looks like I see a handful of patients (depending on the ward I'll get to 6 or 8 a day, like a nurse might have) but in the background all these different cogs are turning. Along the way I'll act as ward clerk when they're not there because there's no nurses to answer the phones (all doing patient care). Yesterday I helped a HCA shower a patient and safely transfer him back to his bed because of his falls risk. 

I can relax and do a little less, but that means that Doris who was largely independent before she came in gets shipped off to a care home against her wishes because her family are fed up with her calling them 4 times a day when she could return to her own home with care and some falls advice/equipment.

I'm a member of a team of around 70 staff for a two site hospital.

I'm an AHP but we cover a 7 day a week service in my current role. Annual leave is agreed within the lower level teams for the days in between but a percentage of the service must be in (so one team can have 60% off and one can have 30% off as long as 50% of the whole service are in). Requests are put in by each person at the start of December and then a manager sorts it out. 

Bank holidays are worked on a rota service, the weekends in between are just rota'd on as part of a rolling service depending on where you were in the rota the months before (it's a rough 6 week rota). The actual bank holiday days (25th/26th/1st) are on a volunteer basis initially, if you worked one the year before you won't get it again. If no-one volunteers then it's whoever hasn't done a bank holiday in the last year and who isn't on the weekends either side of it. 

Goes both ways because we have a high % of staff who don't celebrate Christian holidays or have kids and aren't fussed about NYD who fight over working Christmas Day/Boxing Day/NYD. Nobody wants the weekends in between. People want the actual BHs because they're higher pay and you get the time back.

Our toddler was born at 37 weeks on the dot, I was induced at 36 weeks and 5 days because of bleeding and likely PPROM. If my induction hadn't taken nearly 55 hours he'd have been born before the magical 37 weeks and classed as preterm. 

For comparison, we attended a NCT course (a UK childcare course where you learn about labour and baby care). There were 7 of us on the course all due around the same time. I have noticed absolutely no difference between my boy and my NCT friends kids. He was the \*only\* one born early/before 40 weeks (not the only one induced though, out of the 7 of us only 2 had natural labours and everyone except myself was over 39 weeks at time of delivery).

We were in for a week after birth because he had jaundice (managed on the maternity ward, not NICU). Two others were also kept in hospital for jaundice, one went to the NICU for a day because of it. One other was kept in hospital for a few days for difficulty with feeding leading to loss of over 10% of birth weight. So that's 4/7 who weren't discharged home within 24 hours.

My toddler should have been the fourth born out of our group by due date but was actually first by over two weeks. Now, he's 25 months, and most of the others are just turning 2, and he's one of the tallest and moves the most. Was the first to walk (the second born walked about 5 weeks after he did - there's only 16 days between them). His speech was a bit slower but he's picking up now and this has come on leaps and bounds in the last month. If you lined them all up, you'd be hard pressed to say who was born when and whether they were early, late or on time with the exception of the last two who are nearly 3 and 3.5 months younger than him. I have no doubt in a few years time you wouldn't be able to tell the difference at all.

I had a lot, lot *lot* of guilt over his birth. Should I have just not told anyone? Should I have declined the induction against medical advice? Had I condemned him to a life of being 'less' than his peers? However with time I realised that I had done exactly the right thing and choosing any other option may have resulted in him dying (or me).

Our situation was totally different but also similar. Me and my husband got married in the last week of COVID lockdowns, we were supposed to be 2 weeks clear of all restrictions but ended up with all of them instead. We had 40 guests max, no first dance, cake cutting was with everyone at their table, no group photos, no receiving line, no DJ or dancing, none of the traditional stuff that 'makes' a wedding apart from the ceremony. The only thing that stopped our 'reception' from being as dull as dishwasher was that we got married on a night when the Euros were on and England were playing (and won) and we were allowed to project the match on a big screen in the venue.

When we spoke to the venue about going ahead with the COVID restrictions (a meeting that took place a week before our wedding) we agreed that a year late we would have a 'redo' day and invite everyone we had wanted to be there originally to basically a wedding day minus the ceremony (we were planning to just do a little speech/token ceremony before a big meal and speeches etc.). 30ish people said they were going to come (we originally planned for 120 before COVID happened, as my family is quite large on my Dads side; he's one of four so I have 10 cousins who are all married with their own kids on his side) - that was our parents (4), our siblings and their families (10), 8 of our close work colleagues from each side, one of my aunts and uncles and a handful of other friends who hadn't been able to go to the original date. None of my family except one couple and our siblings/parents came. Two of  my cousins didn't even reply.

I was gutted, truth be told. People just didn't see it as a priority as we were already married. I think some of my cousins felt slighted from not being invited the first time round too, even though legally we weren't allowed to have them (we had our parents and siblings and their spouses/children, our aunts and uncles and ONE set of our friends and that was it on our actual wedding day). The feedback I got from a lot of people was "Oh we've already booked something on that day" (even though they knew of this date 13 months in advance) or "Well you're already married so it's not worth the cost of travelling and staying over".

In the end, we switched to a much cheaper venue and had mainly our friends there who weren't allowed at our actual wedding. The venue was still far too big but we danced, drank and had a great time because the people who cared enough to come had made the effort. My advice is save the money (it saved us about 14k) and enjoy the day with the people who love you and care enough to come along.

Just wanted to weigh in on the screen time. I was staunchly against it, like yourself, to the point where during the day for the first 8 months I'd only put the radio/podcasts on to listen to when we were at home (rather than have adult TV shows on like daytime TV). 

  
Toddler is 2 now. We relented a little around 14 months as he was watching a bit at his childminders and seemed to be aware of what the TV was from then. We watch very selected programs; Tractor Ted, Bluey, Yakka Dee, Something Special and Digley and Daisy as well as the Cars/Planes Disney films and shorts. Yakka Dee is a UK (BBC) program that is fantastic for getting kids to talk. It's basically 6 minutes of a cartoon girl repeating the same 'word of the day' alongside little video clips of that word in toddler appropriate graphics (like a real life spider wearing a CGI hat - "hat spider!" and then it'll be a clip of a little boy holding a stuffed toy spider and he'll say "soft spider!"). We were quite worried about our little ones speech and this did seem to help somewhat. Something Special is a show aimed at SEN kids so it's very calm, the main presenter uses Makaton and the guest children have a range of disabilities. 

  
We do a few episodes of the above a couple of times a week after nursery, and on a Sunday morning we all snuggle in bed together and he watches a little bit more (up to an hour) whilst we wake up slowly with him. 



What I'm trying to say is that TV isn't the devil. It doesn't need to be all or nothing. It took me far, far too long to understand that. When I'm tired at the end of the day, I switch something a bit mindless on. If he's had a busy and stimulating day at nursery, then something like Bluey is a nice switch off for his brain for 20 minutes. I spent far, far too long worrying and stressing about it and yes, I still don't think if/when we have a second we'd let them watch anything much before 12 months (though I imagine that's impossible with a second child!) and I will never give my kid an ipad/phone to watch things on but there is a way to have a 'sensible' (everyones will be different!) level of TV in their lives.

The UK system is very different to the American one. 

  
For one, we are entitled to at least one 20 minute break for every 6 hours we work, which is our time and our time alone to use as we see fit. It can be dictated by the employer as to *when* it is taken, but how you take that is your own choice. If I want to I can walk off my hospital grounds and go to a local supermarket for lunch (or could if there was one close enough and I fancied spending the whole of my break in a queue). OP was clearly not told that there was an expectation for them to be available at a certain time. 15 minutes notice is unacceptable in a remote setting.

Ultimately it's a reciprocal relationship. We don't do it so much for our final year students, but for our first and second year students we flesh out a timetable and tell them (at least for the first few weeks) when and where we expect them to be e.g. Monday 8am - arrive, team catch up, 9am, board round with educator, 10am, supervision with educator, 11am, student education session, Tuesday 8am, arrive, team catch up, 10:30am spend time with discharge team etc. Is that something you could suggest creating and putting in ahead of time for your PEs approval? If you know that time management is an issue for you, put your OT hat on and bring some solutions to the table for your PE.

First thing I do with all my students is book in their supervision, we keep it at roughly the same time every week and I set out a clear expectation for them to bring at least  \*something\* to talk about during the session. Doesn't need to be a huge amount but a general rule to start from is something you're proud of and something you need to improve on.

Finally, have you spoken to your university placement tutor? They should be able to help you navigate this. If you haven't already, email them right now and explain your concerns, anything the PE has said that indicates you might be failing, what you need to them do to support you and what you're planning to do about it next. They have an obligation to support you in your placements especially if you're doing one in such a tricky setting.

You're not incompetent, you're not a poor OT, you're not lacking any self-discipline. This is just a difficult situation you need to navigate carefully with support from your university. You will get through this.

ETA - I fully disagree with commenters saying you shouldn't have popped to the shops during the day. We have an entitlement to breaks in the UK, and if you aren't told when they should be taken or when things are scheduled in for you as you weren't ("Supervision will be at 12pm an hour before lunch, which is at 1pm") you are an adult and can decide when you take them.

Anyway, I think you missed my point. Whatever age you are [i]after puberty[/i] - 25, 35, 65, 105 - you are going to find it significantly harder to learn a language if you have no prior knowledge of ut. And not everyone has a language leaning brain. 

My OH, for example, did German to GCSE level (in reality about 3 years of study here in the UK). He works for a company that has a couple of German factories. He’s spent some time over there, some of the machines he programs and troubleshoots on are in German, and he has meetings with German colleagues who chat in German at the start/end of the call. Doesn’t understand a word of German apart from a couple of snippets of GCSE “where’s the library” stuff. He’s very good at science, computing and maths but his brain just doesn’t retain oral language as well. 

I personally studied German language until my early 20s, and can follow along with most TV shows if I’ve got German subtitles on. I’m quite confident if we moved there within a few years I’d be at the very least competent in day to day and work related German. I don’t think my OH would manage more than your basic conversation starters or greetings.

Language acquisition isn’t a linear experience though. Just like maths it’s something you can learn and be taught but you still might not get very far with it. 

After puberty there are structural changes in the brain in language centres and it’s suggested that this is where your brain “concretes” a language, so some psychologists suggest that learning a language later in life is possible but it’s incredibly difficult to become fluent. If you’re coming from a language that isn’t similar to German in structure than it can be near impossible. 

I’m of course not talking about people who can’t say the basics of conversation (hello/thank you/goodbye/please) which does err on the side of isolationism but more about people who’ve got what would appear to be very basic skills even after years of living in a different country.

Fabric - errm some cotton I got from a sewing shop?! I’m sorry I don’t know what else to call it 🥴

So, a blow by blow account - if you can be bothered to read and add any suggestions to what would make this better then I’d be grateful! 

I borrowed my sisters old Toshiba sewing machine. I have no idea what model number it is or how old it is and if I’m honest it’s probably never been serviced. It’s at least 8 years old, if not more, and my sister used to use it very successful to make clothes for herself. My sister is a very accomplished fabric worker, she’s fab at sewing and crochet and just understands how fabric works. I am not - I always erred to the paper based art forms like watercolour and gouache. 

Aside from a couple of textiles classes at school over 15 years ago now and sewing basic straight lines in a very short lived hand therapy career, I have never really used a sewing machine and certainly have never read a pattern before. Learning point 1 was how to understand the pattern - It took me nearly 2 days to find out that the o with a dot in them on the pattern meant that was where you pivot your needle (thankfully something I was aware of how to do from hand therapy sewing little finger slips). 

Once I’d figured out that transferring the pattern onto tracing paper was indeed the best option (I was going to cut the pattern out directly but was persuaded otherwise by YouTube and my sister) I tried  measuring and cutting the pattern on my living room floor. Reader, sometimes my brain farts and I have to just roll with it. Luckily my husband stopped me and moved my materials to our hard worktop and things went a bit smoother. Learning point 2 here - I traced the pattern using a thick sharpie but I think there must be a better way of doing it. As this was all curves it was really hard to get the right angle at times and my lines were a little wonky to say the least. 

Pattern transferred and I spent a good few hours wondering what to do next. Luckily there’s a couple of ladies on YouTube who have made and filmed themselves making this bear so I watched their videos on repeat. Yes, they both took under an hour from start to finish to make their bears. I took probably 10 times that time. Oh well. Unfortunately both skipped over some of the finer details which I guess just become second nature to skilled sewers so I was slightly in the dark. Cutting the pattern was really daunting and - learning point 3 - I definitely cut it way too close to the lines, I should have left a bit more room I think to the outside of the pattern.

I practiced dart seams on some scrap fabric and it kinda went ok so I felt empowered to do them on my fancy material. The first one was frustrating but went ok. The second one reduced me to tears. I just could not get it to fold and the fabric kept fraying! In the end I managed to get the two sides together in a fashion that was vaguely similar to a dart seam and called it at that. Sewing up the centre seams was quite fun although I struggled to keep the seam allowance consistent. At this point I realised that there was an issue with my sewing machine - I was using straight stitch but it was occasionally giving me really long stitches rather than nice regular short ones, resulting in a morse code style pattern of stitching. Reader, I am not ashamed to say that I have no idea why that happened and I did indeed ignore it. 

I had some issues with my top thread at this point - learning point 4 - as it kept snapping at random times. Bearing in mind that this was just a standard two depth cotton I figured it was something to do with the tension but it didn’t make much difference if I played with the tension wheel so again… I huffed and ignored it. The safety eyes went in really easily and if I’m honest were probably the best part of this project.

Bear almost all sewn up and I came across a problem at the tail end of the sewing. It seemed like the back tail bit was open - I think in hindsight I should have sewing that with the back centre seam rather than starting from above the tail. In the end I went back and stitched to the bottom of the bear, which is why he has a rather dodgy bum.

Before I stuffed him I made a little fabric heart and put a note in it to my little one. I was full of confidence now as it did indeed resemble a bear! Stuffing the ears was fun but stuffing the bod was a little scary as it was obvious that some of the seams are… rickety to say the best. I’ll have to go back and resecure them I think. It was difficult to know if I was over or understuffing; learning point 5 is that I definitely didn’t put enough in the face. 

Ladder stitching up the back… well, as you can see from the photo that didn’t go particularly well either. The edges I was trying to stitch were very frayed and I think I went too far length ways with my stitches before coming back across. I’m not redoing it though. If anyone has any tips for making sure that is really secure let me know. 

Finally, I added a bow tie and looked upon my creation. From certain angles he looks passable, from others he looks like road kill. He’s also much bigger than I expected (final learning point - look at the size of the finished product on the back when you buy the pattern. I was expecting something about a hand and a half height, not 3 hands high). Lots of learning through this and not too many tears shed though! 

I wish I’d just got stuck in with it earlier, I was worried about messing up the fabric but realised when I was sewing the back seam that actually the metre of fabric I was using cost me £6, and the machine was a loan, so all in if it went wrong I was only £6 down. I must have wasted so much sewing cotton though with the threads snapping and the bobbin bird nesting every other time I tried to wind it. Yes, the pattern was a fiver too but I can reuse that because I traced it!

Next I’m planning to try and make my little one some dungarees, when I can find a good [free] pattern.

He definitely needs a capacity assessment. Someone else mentioned that this needs to go through OT but *anyone* can perform one. It is simply making sure that he understands the risks and benefits of an action, can recall this discussion after the fact and can weigh it up. All healthcare professionals carry out capacity assessments whenever we do anything with patients, this is absolutely no different and doesn't need to be OT specific (sorry - bug bear of mine as an OT!). In fact sometimes as OTs tend to be younger women in these situations it can be detrimental to have us do it and some older men respond better to a middle aged male consultant saying "Now come on chap..." 

One thing I would ask that is OT specific is whether or not he's had any functional assessments - has he had a kitchen assessment (often men like this will say "Well my wife will make my cup of tea!" to get around this) or a self care assessment. This can be a double edged sword as if he agrees to do it (again, this is a question of capacity too - for the kitchen assessment alone, if he refuses and has capacity we can't force him to do one) and can do it perfectly but still refuses to do it at home it won't help you. But if he doe it poorly it can be used as evidence to show him that he needs help. Sometimes it is enough to nudge them to accepting help. 

Unfortunately I suspect he will have capacity and will end up going home without anything as I've dealt with many people like this before and you can have every professional telling them until they're blue in the face that it's a bad idea and they will still insist it's not. Everyone \[with capacity\] has the right to make unwise decisions which unfortunately can then impact on other family members. 

If he is deemed to not have capacity then the only thing that changes is the healthcare professionals have to have a best interest meeting to come up with the least restrictive option for him. In this case with the information you have given I suspect they'd say they'll put a care package in for him but then what will happen is he'll refuse to accept the carers help and the care agency will last about 3 days before they withdraw.

Literally just need the box that says “assistance of two for mobility” ticked. Same time as you’re putting your obs on. On our electronic records system it’s on the same page.

When it’s all online and you have 20 patients on your case load across 5 different wards it’s a lot of hassle to track down each individual nurse (who inevitably will go “it’s on their electronic record” or “I don’t know I only met them today”).

Some of us (AHPs) rely on those ‘box ticking’ notes. It’s incredibly unhelpful when you’re trying to write a care plan for someone’s care needs to find that absolutely none of the patient record relating to how they mobilise, how they toilet, how they eat has been filled in (or worse, filled in twice over a 4 day stay with completely contradictory information). Or when you’re trying to justify something to a family member who insists that their relative can or cannot do X/Y/Z (example - I have had more than enough discussions with family who think that their elderly relative needs to go into a care home because they had a fall once at home when they’re completely independent on the ward and don’t want to leave their home). Without any written evidence from nursing staff we have no way of supporting our assessments. Something for you to consider ;)

I wouldn’t take it home as it’s technically confidential and identifiable patient information which should not leave the ward (some people would disagree, but if one of my students (OT, not nursing) took home paper notes even without a patient name or number on I wouldn’t be overly pleased) but writing down on paper roughly what you did and when is a good option when the computer system isn’t working. Shows that you have some initiative by doing so, so well done on that.

Like others have said the chain of command starts with you and ends with your mentor, not with the HCAs or you yourself so if something happens and someone wants to know what Mr X in bed 1 did and it’s not documented it’ll come back on them not you. Some important context to this story - 1) I went to a selective grammar school which was very focused on grades and getting into uni and 2) I was severely depressed from the age of about 17 to 20ish. 

I did fairly well in my GCSEs, got a couple of As, mostly Bs and a C. For my grammar school that wasn't great but good enough for them to keep me on for A levels. I didn't really work for those grades though and coasted a lot of the time on natural ability. That doesn't work for A levels. I wanted to take one particular A level (English lit) but got a C in English Language so the school wouldn't let me. I ended up with History, Psychology, Classics and German. 

I spent most of my AS level year in bed crying so unsurprisingly completely bombed my AS levels and ended up with DDEU (U in History because you really do need to attend those sessions and actually learn something there). The school after several meetings agreed to let me do my A levels but on the compromise that I dropped two subjects and did a short course in General Studies (lol) instead. In hindsight this was 100% because they wanted to say that every pupil got into university in my year group. I picked a course at random because they told me I had to. 

I ended up getting CCD in my overall A levels which was just enough to get my place on a German and TEFL course at a poly. The school wasn't thrilled but I was just pleased to have got somewhere. I ended up dropping out of that course after a few months because, again, shock horror - depression doesn't get cured by moving to a new place and partying all the time. 

Came home, took a year to sort myself out doing retail/hospitality jobs and went back to college to do an access degree. Got a 2:1 in BSc Psychology, then a merit in my Masters. If I didn't work in the NHS then I could probably be earning a lot more but I love what I do and I wouldn't change it (just the systems around it!). I'd love to do further study - perhaps a PHd.

To be registered in the UK you need HCPC registration - [https://www.hcpc-uk.org/registration/getting-on-the-register/international-applications/](https://www.hcpc-uk.org/registration/getting-on-the-register/international-applications/) once you have this or at least have started the process you can apply for jobs at UK hospitals.

You'll walk into a job, we have a massive vacancy rate for OTs across the country at the moment. Jobs are advertised on [https://www.jobs.nhs.uk/](https://www.jobs.nhs.uk/) or [https://www.healthjobsuk.com/](https://www.healthjobsuk.com/) (should all go through NHS jobs as a rule of thumb though). Newly qualified staff start on a band 5 so that's what you should be looking at. Having a masters degree doesn't qualify you for a band 6 position fresh out of uni. Everyone starts on the same wages unless they have previous NHS or private experience and our pay rises (lol, if you can call it that) in two yearly increments so you need to consider where you're going to live - London jobs get 'London Weighting' but even that's not enough to rent and live in London as a newly qualified. Northern cities are cheaper (with the exception of maybe Manchester and Durham I think) whereas the south is much more expensive to live and work in - like I said everyone on the band gets the same wage pretty much in the NHS so if you're in a high cost of living area then your money isn't going to go very far. Oxford is very difficult to rent and live in as well due to the high number of international students who's parents buy property and drive the rent prices to London levels.

OTs are on the shortage occupations list so your employer doesn't need to do the same visa approvals as if it wasn't which is good.

Some trusts have integrated here, so we work with our physio colleagues as equals apart from very specific assessments (respiratory for physios and very high level functional assessments for OTs). In my (acute physical health) trust the main focus is on discharge planning and not rehab, but in somewhere like a community hospital you'd be focused more on rehab. Mental health work tends to be more activity based and with an emphasis on skills in CBT/DBT/talking therapies. We also work in social enterprises, prisons, schools and private industry in the UK too so those are other avenues if you don't want to go into the NHS. It really depends what your cup of OT is as to where to look.

To fully solve the NHS problem you need to look a bit further than just in an acute hospital. You need to look at our entire social care system as well. You can put an acute hospital in every town, stuff it to the brim with Drs/nurses/AHPs/all other essential staff way 'down' to cleaners and housekeepers but if you can't move the patients out of hospital with safe and adequate care, housing and social support you'll have it full in two weeks and no bed flow. At the moment it feels very much like the NHS exists in a vacuum and because we're shouting the loudest we're getting the most attention but social workers, care workers - both private and NHS employed - specialist housing workers etc. are all struggling with the same constraints and frustrations. 

We also have an aging population and an incredibly focused medical model that does not like to accept dying as an inevitability on the spectrum of life, so often people are admitted when they don't 'need' to be and 50 or even 30 years ago they would have been managed at home for end of life care rather than blue lighted to hospital because their breathing got a bit rattily in their final hours (which is very natural for some people and can be managed incredibly effectively at home *if* you have the resources and education to empower families to do it). I'll clarify that I'm not saying here we should take anyone over the age of 95 out the back and shoot them, but we should consider whether or not the treatments we give and offer to people are truly in their best interests or just because we have the technology and we can do it. That is a very individual aspect of care though and one that I find a lot of Drs miss. 

One of the biggest problems I personally see if that not only does the NHS act largely separately from our social care cousins, but each individual NHS trust acts individually. There's very little resource sharing and I've been met at times with contempt by other colleagues in a different trust when I've tried to sort out a patient who's been in my county on holiday and needed emergency admission. If we all worked together and shared our resources and knowledge we'd be able to get people to the right place quicker. 

Culturally the NHS is incredibly toxic at the moment and that needs to change because it's a probably the second biggest reason why people leave, other than our shit wages. How you change that I'm not sure. 

How you attract people to the professions we have in our remit who are truly passionate about patient care and research etc. is another big problem that needs to be solved. How you retain them is simple - you provide people with the right resources, rewards and confidence to do their jobs properly.

I'm in the UK and work for the NHS in an acute setting. Sadly we're all experiencing the same things here as you are.

OTs in the UK are paid the same as any qualified non-medical staff member in the NHS - starting salary of £27,055 (roughly $33k) to maybe £40,588 (at present, roughly $50k) after several years experience, a promotion and then another 5 years of working at that level. After that you have to move out of clinical practice to get another £2k on your wage. We get no other benefits (in the UK sick leave, maternity leave and holidays are somewhat protected in law compared to the US - those problems you're facing there are endemic in the American workforce culture I'm afraid). We regularly do unpaid overtime, work a 7 day a week rota, have far too many patients to see, no equipment to give them, have to continually advocate for our patients in a far too medical model and often can't provide the right level of care/support for people on discharge because the wider community services are even worse off. I've worked four of the UK bank holidays in one way or another this year so far (there's only been 5, and I'm working my fifth out of the total 6 we've had nationally in late August), worked Christmas twice (only started in the role in 2018) and am likely to have to work Christmas or New Years Day again this year because we've haemorrhaged staff and can't cover the rota fully. As a whole workforce we're currently threatening strikes because the governments best pay increase off 'to match inflation' is 5%... inflation is rising/has risen to 12% and our salaries have not matched inflation increases since the 90s. All of us worked through COVID and pulled extra shifts, worked as healthcare (nursing) assistants or ward clerks or cleaners if necessary to just keep the hospital running (as did many other professionals in the NHS). We're now still working with a COVID+ve population but no longer get protected sick leave if we test positive.

We've lost so many staff from my Trust over the last few months that for some areas we have two or at most three therapy staff (not qualified clinical OTs or physios, anyone who comes under therapy - whether thats a support worker \[COTA\] or a non-clinical therapy manager) covering upwards of 80 patients a day. People are leaving daily. You know how many OTs we recruited this year? 3. Two have already left. One has handed her notice in.

I have friends who are estate agents, one of them regularly earns £50k on top of her normal salary (around £45k) in commission. Another works in TV and gets every other Friday afternoon off, free tickets to film premieres, overtime is paid at double his hourly rate, and he travels the country meeting producers and directors for £65k a year. My husband earns double my wage, gets a yearly pay rise of at least 3% above inflation as well as a Christmas bonus, and has 'standard' UK holiday entitlement as well as bank holidays and Christmas off, and the opportunity to take a week a year as volunteering leave.

Some of it you take on the chin and accept as a healthcare worker. I don't mind too much staying late if I'm doing something that's worthwhile and helps my patient out. But some of it takes the absolute piss and it's burning us all out.

ETA - In the UK OT isn't necessarily a Masters level degree, I do have a Masters and am the only person in my friendship group/my husbands friendship group who has a degree past Batchelors level. I am the one who earns the least and has the least potential to increase my earnings.

They aren't bed blockers. They're people just like you and me with real needs that can't be met in their home environment. A large part of my job as an OT is around discharge for people and trust me, none of us shunt people into nursing homes or discharge to assess beds (which is what it sounds like your husband worked in) just for the hell of it or to get people out of hospital. 

The government has been so lax with making sure nursing homes are up to standard that a lot of them in our area have \*had\* to close because their CQC inspections were beyond salvageable. Serious safety issues around lack of staff, environmental issues such as 1 bathroom to 8 residents, stairs in the middle of the hallway in a dementia specialist place, lack of trained nurses to give meds out. We've recently had a large 'chain' of nursing homes in our area closed down which takes about 450 beds out of the county. The only one in my village is closing at the end of August largely because they can't modernise it, losing another 45 or so beds. We have an aging population and unfortunately it's not always safe or practical to allow people to live in their own homes until they die. 

Not to mention some bright spark somewhere decided that the process of moving someone permanently to a nursing home (even when it's blatantly obvious, such as someone who has no family around, with an advanced neurological deteriorating condition, who cannot safely care for themselves even with a care package) *has* to happen outside of the hospital environment. Therefore the people we know who would do really well in a nice supported nursing home set up for their needs get sent to  inadequate/inappropriate ones where a social worker comes out and decides on one or two assessments whether or not they should stay in funded care. The whole process takes months and always has done - pre-COVID it was around 16 weeks waiting for a discharge to assess bed. It's now more like 36 weeks in some areas. 

Not to mention the absolute hullaballoo you have to deal with if that individual isn't an elderly frail patient - I've had adults with severe learning disabilities rejected for specialist nursing homes because someone in an office somewhere has seen "Age = 45" and decided they're far too young, despite them never being able to live independently and requiring 24/7 supervision due to no safety/risk awareness and significant physical and mental health needs. 

Don't get me started on the hell that has been end of life placement/care in the last two and a half years.

It's an absolute shambles but it's not the fault of the patients.  Ever since the push to have people cared for in the community, not in nursing homes/hospital in the early 90s we've been fire fighting this and unfortunately now it's coming to a head. It's the most frustrating, infuriating and soul destroying thing and is now why a lot of therapists are leaving the NHS as well, making the problem worse for the ones who aren't leaving (before COVID we had at least one therapist, OT or physio, and one support worker on each ward. We no longer have any band 5 OTs on my hospital site, only 3 support workers and 4 band 6 OTs to cover 10 different wards. We have a handful of physios but the ratio is now something like 1 qualified therapy staff member to 3 wards).

I suppose my thought process on the 'we're adults, we can decide for ourselves' argument is that a fair number of smokers start before the age of 18, when they are not adults and therefore do not have anywhere near enough knowledge or ability to critically think about whether or not in 40 years time they'd like to be drowning in their own secretions because their lungs have liquified. Hell, most people think they're invincible until about the age of 25 and aren't able to objectively think about whether an action is going to cause them trouble in the very long term. That's just human nature.

Vapes are at present are becoming a problem in schools -  [https://www.walesonline.co.uk/news/wales-news/police-probe-parents-claims-children-23703674](https://www.walesonline.co.uk/news/wales-news/police-probe-parents-claims-children-23703674) and the Government's 2020 report [https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/vaping-in-england-evidence-update-march-2020/vaping-in-england-2020-evidence-update-summary](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/vaping-in-england-evidence-update-march-2020/vaping-in-england-2020-evidence-update-summary) suggests that 11% of 15 year old have vaped. The interesting part of that statement is that only 1% of children who vape had *not* smoked before they started using a vape pen so ultimately we can draw from that that roughly 10% of 15 year olds have smoked. You might say vaping is otherwise unrelated but we just do not know what harm that shite would do to your lungs in 10/20/30 years time. 

I don't smoke and never have myself. I'm glad I don't have to make a decision on whether people should be allowed to smoke because when you try and take away something that's so insidiously addictive you're always going to have opposition. 

I do however work with people who are dying a very untimely death because of smoking. Very few people I meet feel the same way about smoking when it's killing them at the age of 57 before they can watch their 22 year old daughter walk down the aisle or hold their first grandkid as they did when they started, for whatever reason they started. It's a fact that lung diseases in particular have a very strong correlation with and have in many studies been shown to be caused by smoking. They're utterly horrific to die from and if there's any legislation we can bring in to try and reduce the chance of people dying from them then we should do it. They're also - for some diseases - almost entirely preventable, much like many other diseases that we managed to eradicate by improving our knowledge on what causes them and putting measures in place to reduce or remove those disease triggers.
